Morning light spills through my kitchen window at a slant now, September's angle, and I find myself watching dust motes in that beam like I did as a child. Some things we never outgrow, only forget to notice.

I've been thinking about how we carry places with us. My grandmother's kitchen smelled of simmering tomatoes and wooden spoons worn soft at the edges. I don't have her recipe, exactly—she never wrote anything down—but sometimes my hands know the motion of stirring, the weight of a pinch of salt, and something in my chest unlocks. The body keeps its own archives.

We talk so much about moving forward, as if time were a corridor with a single direction. But I think we orbit. The same sorrows, the same small joys, circling back transformed. Grief doesn't resolve so much as it changes orbit, becomes a moon instead of a sun, still tugging at the tides.

Last week I heard a woman laughing on the bus, that particular helpless wheeze when something catches you off-guard, and I felt an absurd gratitude. Strangers' unguarded moments—the way someone reads a letter, the particular slouch of relief when they think no one's watching—these feel like stolen gifts, reminders that we're all performing interior lives no audience will ever fully witness.

What I want to say, maybe, is that attention is the last real currency. Noticing the particular blue of evening coming on. The way a dog sleeps with absolute trust. How rain on different surfaces makes different languages. We're dying from the first moment; this isn't morbid, just the frame that makes the painting matter. Choose your focal points carefully. The dust motes. The light.
